title: Stationarity: why a series gets differenced
intro: Forecasting models learn from the past and carry what they learned into the future. Carrying it over only makes sense while the rules of the game stay the same: the mean holds its place, the spread does not grow, the link between neighbouring days is the same at the start and at the end. A series with that property is called stationary. Growing revenue does not have it — and it is brought into shape by moving from the values themselves to their increments.

beats.text: Below the chart run two gauges: a rolling mean and a rolling spread, both over a two-week window. That is the eyeball test for stationarity. On the raw series the mean line crawls steadily upwards — the series is growing, so its mean depends on the moment you look at it.

The d = 1 button switches the series to its first difference: instead of «how much there was that day» it shows «how much it changed since yesterday». The trend disappears: steady growth of 0.6 per day turns into a constant addition of 0.6 that the series simply wobbles around.
beats.predict: What happens to the rolling-mean gauge after the first difference?
beats.reveal: It flattens out: the increments oscillate around a constant level, and the mean line loses its direction. This is exactly what the letter I in ARIMA means — integrated: the model works not with the series itself but with its differences, and then adds the forecast back up.

beats.text: A difference can also be taken at the seasonal lag — the «seasonal difference» button. Then each day has the same weekday one week earlier subtracted from it: Monday minus last Monday.
beats.predict: Which part does such a difference remove, and what happens to the weekly sawtooth on the chart?
beats.reveal: Seasonality goes away: identical weekdays share the same seasonal addition, and subtracting cancels it. The sawtooth disappears. An ordinary difference fights the trend, a seasonal one fights the cycle; they are different tools and are taken independently of each other.

beats.text: It is tempting to take more differences and make the series completely flat. That is a bad idea.
beats.predict: Set d = 2 and look at the amplitude of the series and at the spread gauge. What changed compared with d = 1?
beats.reveal: The swings grew noticeably: each difference subtracts one random value from another, and the noise variance adds up. The series becomes flatter in its mean but noisier in its spread — and noise cannot be forecast. The practical rule: d = 1 almost always, d = 2 rarely, more than that almost never.

beats.text: The formal check for stationarity is the Dickey — Fuller test (ADF) and its relatives. Its null hypothesis is «the series is non-stationary», so a small p-value means non-stationarity has been rejected. This is a rare case where rejecting the null is the good news, and it is easy to get the direction of the conclusion wrong.

So the series has been taken apart, checked for memory and brought to a stationary form. Next comes forecasting itself, starting with methods that require none of those checks: the moving average and exponential smoothing.

definitions.text: the property of a series whose mean, spread and structure of dependence between observations do not change over time.
moving from the values of a series to their increments; removes the trend.
subtracting the value exactly one period earlier; removes seasonality.
how many times a series was differenced to make it stationary; the letter I in ARIMA.
a formal check for stationarity; the null hypothesis is that the series is non-stationary, so a small p-value speaks in favour of stationarity.

practice: The routine is standard: look at the chart and the correlogram, take a difference, look again. If after the first difference the correlogram stops decaying slowly, that much differencing is enough.

Automatic selection (auto_arima and friends) picks d by stationarity tests on its own. It is still worth checking: on short series the tests are unstable, and an extra difference costs more than a missing one.

Series in money and in counts are often better logged before differencing. Then the difference of logs reads as a relative increment — «so many percent versus yesterday» — and a spread that grows with the level is stabilised.
realLife: Stock prices are nearly non-stationary, while their daily returns are nearly stationary. That is why finance models the return rather than the price: precisely the move to a difference of logs.
Inflation is published not as a price level but as the increment over the previous period — the same first difference in everyday language.
The «year over year» comparison in reporting is essentially a seasonal difference with period 12: a way to remove the annual cycle and part of the trend in one go.
assumptions: Differencing cures non-stationarity in the mean, but not in the spread. If the size of the swings grows with the level, a transformation comes first — a log or Box — Cox — and only then the difference.

Stationarity is an assumption of the model, not a property of the business. A change in pricing policy, a launch in a new country or a pandemic make the past unfit to carry into the future, and no amount of differencing will fix that: the series has to be cut into periods.
deepDive: There are two kinds of non-stationarity and they are treated differently. A series with a deterministic trend (values wobbling around a straight line) only needs to be cleaned by a regression on time. A series with a stochastic trend — a random walk where each value equals yesterday's plus noise — is not cured by a regression on time, it needs a difference. Confusing them is expensive: an extra difference on the first inflates noise, a missing one on the second leaves false predictability.

The same effect produces spurious regression: take two independent random walks, regress one on the other, and R² comes out high with a confidently significant t-statistic — although there is no relationship at all. The famous «correlations» between cheese consumption and the divorce rate live on exactly this: both series simply grow.
